prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse room layout: the ceiling and rear wall are several metres away, while the table edge, laptops, and nearest people are roughly 0.3–1.5 m from the camera wearer; people along the far wall are approximately 2–4 m away and generally farther from one another than the seated group around the table. Across frames 1–5, the closest foreground person shifts from the left edge to the right/centre and back toward the left side of the scene, indicating camera turning rather than a clear sustained approach or retreat; other seated people remain at broadly similar depths. Bright silhouettes make near-person occlusion clearer than RGB, especially where a foreground head or torso blocks people, chairs, and the table behind it, and they show that the tabletop lies below and in front of the people. The map is unreliable for exact metre estimates, merges some adjacent bodies and furniture, loses thin objects and facial orientation, and shows inconsistent brightness on surfaces that appear to be at similar distances.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates multiple people from the dining table, chairs, laptops, and televisions, clarifying which overlapping RGB regions belong to distinct instances; most people are roughly 0.5–2 m from nearby table objects and about 0.5–3 m from one another, but the masks alone do not provide dependable camera-distance measurements. It shows people distributed from far left to far right, with seated or leaning figures behind the table and closer torsos partly cut off by the lower or side image boundaries; laptops sit on the table below and in front of several people, generally within about an arm's reach of those nearest them. Across the five frames, instance positions slide laterally as the camera turns: a large near-person mask moves through the foreground, repeatedly occluding smaller people and objects behind, while the central table group remains in view. The map reveals object boundaries and occlusion ordering that are hard to separate in RGB, but several masks are fragmented, merged, mislabeled, or missing, and it cannot reliably show gaze direction, front-versus-back body orientation, or precise distances.
descriptions.pose: The pose map supports body configuration and facing estimates: most detected upper bodies lie about 1–3 m ahead around the table, with heads above shoulders and arms extending inward or laterally, while magenta hand detections appear close to one foreground person's hands at roughly 0.5–1 m from the camera. Head and shoulder geometry suggests several people are turned sideways toward neighbors or the table, while a few faces in the RGB appear directed approximately toward the camera wearer, but sparse facial landmarks make gaze uncertain. Across the five frames, skeletons move mainly left or right with the camera rotation; some arm configurations change, yet there is no reliable evidence of substantial approach or retreat, and many bodies disappear when occluded by the nearest person or cropped by the frame. The map makes limb overlap, reach, and articulated posture easier to see than RGB—for example, which hands are near a face, torso, or tabletop—but it omits furniture and depth, swaps or breaks joints, produces stray detections, and cannot establish exact inter-person distances or whether an obscured limb lies in front of or behind another object.
